note: Web performance budgets (Task 60f). Every number was MEASURED; each demo records the runs it came from. WHAT IS GATED CHANGED after the first Firefox baseline (see `gatingPolicy`): payload and crossings-per-tick are gated, startup is recorded but NOT gated. Firefox's higher crossings-per-tick on _process-heavy demos is a SETTLED headless-environment artifact, not an engine defect (task 74, 2026-08-03): nothing paces requestAnimationFrame in headless Firefox, so render-frame-driven command emission multiplies while physics-driven work tracks the wall-capped physics step; a display-paced Firefox sits near Chrome. Per-engine budgets bound regressions within each environment's own baseline. TASK 84 (2026-08-10) re-measured charactercontroller, thirdperson and racing: those three had no `mode` branch in the JS bridge's frame dispatch and so took its SPIKE BENCHMARK fallthrough, which appended a synthetic scalar mutation per dispatch and never counted a _process tick. Their old numbers graded the benchmark, not the game -- every one of them moved DOWN on re-measurement and every ceiling tightened. Each carries a `supersedes` string with what it replaced; nothing here was loosened.
headroom: payload +15% (asset growth, not a texture reimport); startup 3x with an 8s floor; crossings/tick 2x with a 2.0 floor -- the ratio is diluted by tick count, so 2x absorbs host variation while a real regression (per-frame work reaching the cross-module path) multiplies it several times over.
builtinCallsNote: Task 129 E review B1, reviewed again for task 138 item 33: immediate builtin / utility calls (bridge.builtinCalls: one synchronous round trip each, 10-30 us, not counted in crossingsPerTick). Every demo is gated PER TICK (builtinCalls / ticksObserved, i.e. the envelope's builtinCallsPerTick; a tick is one script dispatch, so it counts every scripted node) by its own maxBuiltinCallsPerTick or this default; per tick is what caught the fps regression (1.06 per tick against 0.5, 2.1x). A demo whose calls follow SIMULATED time instead declares maxBuiltinCallsPerSimSecond (builtinCalls / simSeconds), which REPLACES its per-tick cap: only bunnymark (GD.randf draws on a spawn; its fixed-length run is ~190 ticks on any host, so a slower host simulates more time per tick and calls per tick rise with load: ~30 ticks per simulated second on a hosted runner against ~55 on a Mac). simSeconds is the game's time, one delta per engine frame (the bridge used to add it once per scripted node, which made it 4-7x game time on dodge and the per-second rate meaningless; fixed in task 138 item 33). Every other demo's calls are a fixed startup count or a small rate per dispatch, and a per-second figure for them reads the run's length, not the program: web3d makes 87 calls whether it runs 2.7 s of game time (Chrome) or 1.2 s (Firefox), 31.8 against 72.5 per simulated second, but 0.060 against 0.089 per tick; fps 31.7 against 78.3 per second, 0.200 against 0.153 per tick. Firefox runs simulate 2-4x less game time than Chrome's for the same demo, so a fixed startup count inflates a per-second rate there. A demo whose tick ratio is exempt (tickRatioNotApplicable) is exempt here too unless it declares a ceiling, and its verdict line says exempt. A record-only engine (safari) still has its builtin calls graded, on the Chrome/Firefox-derived ceilings above (no Safari figure was ever measured): the count is a property of the program (a fixed startup count, or a small rate per dispatch or per spawn), not of how the engine paces requestAnimationFrame, which is what makes crossings per tick record-only there. A Safari run with too few ticks to judge is red too, from the builtin-call check itself: the crossings check that reports that elsewhere is skipped for a record-only engine. Measured 2026-10-14 with the shipped build (macOS arm64, Chrome 155 / Firefox 157 headless, protocol 35; scripts/web_ci_matrix.sh --demo-set ci against the demos commit pinned in web.yml, two full runs), calls per tick, highest of the runs, Chrome | Firefox: racing 0 | 0; charactercontroller 0.004 | 0.001; platformer 0.009 | 0.006; thirdperson 0.004 | 0.001; citybuilder 0.023 | 0.008; dodge 0.016 | 0.011; squash 0.013 | 0.008; tpsdemo 0.076 | 0.030; web3d 0.060 | 0.091; fps 0.245 | 0.153; bunnymark 5.1-6.9 | 5.2-5.3 (per simulated second 283-315 | 306-313); match3 0.77-1.81 | 0.45-1.02, exempt (input-driven). The gating host is the CI runner, which measures higher than a workstation: the web-ci-matrix on main at 1680c4d3 (hosted Linux runner, Chrome and Firefox headless; run 38567206009 and others, evidence in the run artifacts) measured fps on Chrome at 0.26 per tick (156 calls over 610 ticks; 0.23 and 0.22 on the other runs) and 0.10-0.11 on Firefox, against 0.200-0.245 over seven Chrome runs here. The default 0.5 is therefore 1.92x the highest recorded figure (fps on the runner's Chrome, 0.26) and 3.3x the highest on Firefox (0.153 here), not the 2.04x the workstation runs alone suggested; check_budgets.py --self-test asserts at least 1.9x against the highest of the local and CI measurements. It stays 0.5 because the pre-fix fps 1.06 must stay red, and the pre-fix figures stay red: fps 1.06 (2.1x the cap), racing 9.22 (18x), tpsdemo 0.60 and citybuilder 0.52 (just over), while platformer's 0.32 was never over it (check_budgets.py --self-test replays them; those envelopes predate the simSeconds fix, which only the bunnymark ceiling reads).

knownExceptions.tpsdemo: 638 MB served payload, 570 MB of it upstream demo assets in index.pck. It RUNS, but nobody would download it: this is far outside any sane web budget, and the number below records reality rather than blessing it. Fixing it is asset work in the demo (texture compression, trimming), which 60f explicitly puts out of scope -- budgets are not met by editing gameplay or scene content.

bunnymark.builtinCallsBudgetFrom: 2x the 314.78 calls per simulated second, the highest of twelve runs of the shipped build on 2026-10-14 (Chrome 155: 282.95, 293.95, 295.64, 305.51, 307.25, 314.78; Firefox 157: 305.52, 308.56, 309.48, 311.35, 312.54, 312.88; 979-1278 calls over 3.3-4.1 s of game time, 5.1-6.9 per tick): every builtin call is GD.randf / GD.randfRange on a spawn, and spawns follow simulated time. It REPLACES the per-tick cap (default 0.5; bunnymark makes ~5.3 per tick): per tick it moved with the host (6.87 at 45.8 ticks per simulated second, 5.10 at 55.5; a hosted runner ran 166 ticks over 5.54 s, ~30 ticks per second, which puts it near 9.7), per simulated second it moved 10% across both engines, so one ceiling serves Chrome and Firefox. On the CI runner (the gating host; web-ci-matrix on main at 1680c4d3, run 38567206009 and others) it measured 272-314 per simulated second in the two matrix runs kept as evidence (Chrome 1320 calls over 4.2 s = 314.3 and 1464 over 5.38 s = 272.1; Firefox 1002 over 3.24 s = 309.3 and 1008 over 3.3 s = 305.5; the same four are in the check_budgets.py self-test), 7.42-8.77 per tick on Chrome, against this 640: 2.0x the highest rate. The engine's global generator is the RNG on every platform by decision (2026-10-14): one generator shared with GDScript, seeded sequences identical everywhere, so each draw crosses the bridge and this ceiling stays (task 129 E review B1, task 138 item 33).

firefox.budgetFrom: Chrome's number, NOT 2x Firefox's own 0.23. Before task 84 Firefox sat far ABOVE Chrome here (19.58 vs 4.50) because the benchmark transport emitted one synthetic command per dispatch and headless Firefox's unpaced rAF dispatches several times more often. With that gone, the residual crossings are physics-driven (wall-capped) while unpaced rAF only inflates processTicks, so Firefox's ratio now sits BELOW Chrome's and Chrome is the conservative bound for both. The pre-84 CI Firefox figure (12.13) measured the benchmark and is not carried forward; the next full-corpus CI run re-measures it.

match3.tickRatioNotApplicable: Input-driven: the driver spends its run on pointer gestures and settle waits, so the script layer is dispatched only ~20-50 times per run (53 on a local Chrome, 23 on a CI Chrome, 127 on a local Firefox). A ratio whose denominator swings that far with the host is not a measurement, and failing on it would grade the runner -- exactly what these budgets exist to avoid. Payload is still gated.

soak.note: The soak gate drives the dodge export, so its payload budget is dodge's. Its crossings/tick is the most trustworthy ratio in the file -- ~95k ticks, so the fixed startup cost is fully amortised -- which is why its floor for a verdict is 1000 ticks rather than 30.

spike.note: The gated transport benchmark cell (task 84 follow-up). Its transport cost is NOT gated by a ceiling here but STRUCTURALLY by the driver's page_* checks: the OPERATIONS(10000)-mutation batch must cross the boundary exactly ONCE (page_backendQueuedCrossings), with zero command-buffer growths -- exact equalities, tighter than any measured ceiling could be. The observed run counters are engine-stable because the lifecycle is frame-count-structural, not wall-clocked: 186/305 crossings/spikeFrames on Chrome vs 185/304 on Firefox, appliedCommands 260161 vs 260160.
spike.tickRatioNotApplicable: The spike never takes the _process/_physics_process tick paths this ratio counts -- its frames dispatch into kanamaWebEmptyFrame/kanamaWebSpikeProcess, and processTicks === physicsTicks === 0 is itself a driver assertion (realProcessPathNotDispatched, the inverse of the demo drivers' realProcessPathDispatched). A ratio with a structurally zero denominator is not a measurement. Payload is still gated.

gatingPolicy.payloadBytes: GATED. Bytes are host- and engine-independent by construction.
gatingPolicy.startupMs: RECORDED, NOT GATED. It is wall-clock and it does not survive a loaded machine: the same thirdperson build measured 4.4s on an idle Chrome and 64.7s on a Firefox sharing a busy workstation. A gate that red-lights because someone else was compiling is measuring the machine, and the failure it would catch (a demo that stops booting) already shows up as a driver timeout.
gatingPolicy.crossingsPerTick: GATED PER ENGINE. Engine-stable for most of the corpus (bunnymark 2.22/1.97, dodge 0.19/0.20, citybuilder 0.84/0.77, fps 1.10/1.02 for chrome/firefox). The per-engine split was introduced because Firefox measured 5-10x Chrome's ratio on the input-heavy demos (charactercontroller 4.50 -> 19.58, thirdperson 1.15 -> 6.01) and a Chrome-derived budget reddened main. Task 84 (2026-08-10) established that for those three demos the asymmetry was an artifact of the spike-benchmark fallthrough: the synthetic per-dispatch command scaled with Firefox's unpaced rAF. On the real _process path the asymmetry INVERTS (charactercontroller 1.86 -> 0.23, thirdperson 0.29 -> 0.12, racing 2.09 -> 0.68), because the residual crossings are physics-driven and wall-capped while unpaced rAF only inflates processTicks. Those three therefore take Chrome's ceiling on both engines as the conservative bound. The structure stays per-engine: it is still the right shape, and the rest of the corpus was never re-measured under it.

safari.recordOnly: Hand-run local gate (no headless mode, no CI cell) whose ceilings were never measured: every number in this file was derived on Chrome/Firefox. Numbers are recorded for the corpus baseline; add measured safari engine entries and remove this policy to gate them (task 86). Builtin / utility calls are NOT record-only: they are graded on the Chrome/Firefox-derived ceilings, because the count is a property of the program, not of how the engine paces requestAnimationFrame (and a run with too few ticks to judge is red there).
